decision_question: 大学学术写作课是否应该允许学生使用 AI 写作助手（如 ChatGPT）辅助写作并提供形成性反馈？
target_population: university undergraduate students enrolled in academic writing courses
target_context: university academic writing course (16-week semester), scaffolded formative-feedback instruction, instructor feedback available, offline
supported_claims: Using ChatGPT as a formative feedback tool can significantly improve short-term academic writing scores and is positively perceived by students (E-001, E-002).
Guardrail design (hints and feedback instead of answers) eliminates the negative learning effect of unguarded AI access (E-004).
Interactive AI homework can raise engagement and satisfaction without harming learning outcomes (E-007, E-008).
Task/assignment scores must not be equated with independent writing ability (E-003, E-005).
uncertain_claims: Whether AI-assisted writing instruction improves or preserves long-term independent writing ability in university students — no direct evidence; E-003 (subject-mismatched) is the only independent-performance signal.
Whether the 6-hour Marzuki effect extends to a full semester (E-001).
Whether engagement gains from high school ESL homework (Lee) generalize to university academic writing courses (E-007, E-008).
contradicted_claims: The claim that 'AI writing assistants always improve independent writing performance' is contradicted by E-003 (unguarded access → 17% worse independent exam performance).
reason_for_disagreement: Disagreement comes from outcome separation (task/assignment scores vs independent ability), tool design (guarded feedback vs unguarded generation), and population (high school vs university). Writing-context evidence (Marzuki) is positive but short and uncontrolled; the strongest evidence (Bastani) shows unguarded AI harms independent performance but in a different subject and level.
methodology_summary: One mixed-methods university writing study (Marzuki 2024: no randomization, 6-hour intervention, delayed test), one large high-school mathematics RCT (Bastani 2026: task-vs-learning separation, guardrail comparison), and one high-school ESL RCT (Lee 2025: engagement plus non-inferior learning). No randomized university-level academic writing study with a no-AI independent writing transfer test exists in the reviewed set.

outcome_specific_findings.knowledge_gain: positive short-term writing-skill gain with AI feedback (E-001); non-inferior with a significant gain in one group for ESL homework (E-008)
outcome_specific_findings.independent_problem_solving: negative for unguarded access, neutralized by guardrails (E-003, E-004); never measured in a university writing context
outcome_specific_findings.assignment_score: improves during practice but does not transfer to independent performance (E-005)
outcome_specific_findings.engagement: positive for AI interactive homework (E-007) and positive student perceptions of AI feedback (E-002)
outcome_specific_findings.ai_dependency: documented crutch behavior with unguarded access (E-006)

short_term_effect: Positive: AI-assisted formative feedback improves short-term writing scores (E-001) and engagement (E-002, E-007).
long_term_effect: Unknown: no university writing study measures independent writing ability beyond the intervention; Marzuki's delayed test follows only a 6-hour intervention (E-001).
transfer_effect: Negative evidence from mathematics warns that task gains do not transfer to independent performance (E-003, E-005); no university writing transfer test exists.
risk_effect: AI dependency, academic-integrity violations and false confidence are real risks for unguarded usage (E-006); guardrail design mitigates the negative learning effect (E-004).

applicability.suitable_for: bounded pilot in a university academic writing course with a guardrailed AI usage policy and independent no-AI writing assessment
applicability.not_suitable_for: unrestricted student AI use without a usage policy or integrity safeguards
required_conditions: academic integrity policy covering AI-assisted writing

what_can_be_claimed: AI writing assistants used as formative feedback tools can improve short-term academic writing scores and are positively perceived by students.
Unguarded generative AI access carries a real risk of harming independent performance when the AI is removed.
Guardrail design (feedback/hints instead of answers) substantially mitigates that risk.
AI interactive homework can improve engagement without harming learning outcomes.
Direct evidence about university academic writing independent ability is missing.
what_cannot_be_claimed: AI writing assistants improve (or even preserve) university students' long-term independent writing ability.
Any semester-long academic writing outcome based on a 6-hour intervention.
That writing/assignment score gains reflect genuine independent writing skill rather than AI-supported task performance.
Any claim about academic-integrity outcomes, which none of the three studies directly measured.
missing_evidence: Randomized or matched-section study of AI writing assistants in university academic writing courses with a no-AI independent writing transfer test.
Studies varying AI usage policy (guardrailed feedback vs open generation) within a writing course.
Longitudinal data on AI dependency and academic integrity in university writing beyond one course.
Retention evidence for writing outcomes beyond a few weeks.
decision_rationale: Writing-context evidence is positive but short and uncontrolled; strong general evidence warns that unguarded AI harms independent performance; and no university writing study measures independent ability. A bounded, guardrailed, 4-phase pilot with an independent no-AI writing transfer test is the evidence-consistent action.
exceeds_evidence_boundary: 'AI 写作助手能提高大学生的独立写作能力' — exceeds: no university writing study measures independent no-AI writing ability.
'AI 写作助手对学术诚信无风险' — exceeds: no reviewed study measured academic-integrity outcomes.
'AI 辅助写作的分数提升等于写作能力提升' — exceeds: task performance and independent ability are demonstrably distinct (E-003, E-005).
